page: Vultr vhp-4c-8gb-amd is a virtual server instance categorized within the High Performance family, configured with a 1:2 memory-to-vCPU ratio. It features 4 shared vCPUs derived from 2 physical cores on an AMD EPYC processor running at a base clock frequency of 2.0 GHz. The processor includes 32 KB of L1 data cache, 0.5 MB of L2 cache, and 16 MB of L3 cache, alongside support for AVX, AES, SHA-NI, and BMI2 instruction sets. System memory is sized at 8.0 GB, equating to 2.0 GB per vCPU. No dedicated GPU hardware is included. Storage is bundled as a single 180 GB local NVMe SSD, and networking is provisioned with one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark outcomes show mid-tier raw CPU compute capacity coupled with bottlenecks in uncached memory throughput and general data processing. Under stress-ng, the instance achieves average results with 2306.16 in single-core and 9232.12 in multi-core metrics. PassMark CPU encryption performs solidly at 3693.88, assisted by hardware-level AES and SHA extensions. In contrast, Geekbench results fall into lower percentiles, recording a single-core score of 1119.0 and a multi-core score of 3378.0. Large-block uncached memory operations register 17.9 GB/sec read and 12.56 GB/sec write bandwidth, contributing to weak outcomes in PassMark memory (870.44) and database operations (919.74).

Given its shared-core execution model and constrained uncached memory throughput, this instance is suited for lightweight compute tasks, small-scale utility microservices, staging environments, and entry-level automation workers. The bundled 180 GB NVMe volume provides ample local drive space without secondary attachment overhead, though heavy memory-bound tasks and high-throughput transactional database engines should be avoided.
description: Vultr vhp-4c-8gb-amd is a shared-core compute instance within Vultr's High Performance family, providing 4 vCPUs across 2 physical AMD EPYC cores clocked at 2.0 GHz, 8.0 GB of system memory, and a bundled 180 GB local NVMe SSD. It features x86_64 architecture with hardware instruction support for AES, SHA-NI, and AVX, without dedicated GPU acceleration. Benchmark data demonstrates standard synthetic compute throughput on stress-ng tests, alongside mid-range cryptographic acceleration. However, uncached memory bandwidth is comparatively restricted at 17.9 GB/sec read and 12.56 GB/sec write, resulting in lower scores on database operations and web serving benchmarks. This configuration provides a functional balance of compute resources and local NVMe capacity for lightweight application serving, CI/CD runners, internal tool hosting, and pre-production staging workloads that do not demand persistent high-memory bandwidth.
